projectOutComesReport:
Increasingly erratic climatic and environmental conditions are negatively impacting communities around the world. This is especially pronounced in many coastal areas where sustainability of fisheries and fragile marine ecosystems is under severe strain. The deep-time perspective offered by archaeology provides one means by which to assess the impacts of climatic and environmental change on human communities, as our species has learned to cope with a variety of extreme conditions throughout the world for hundreds-of-thousands of years. 

 

The results of this dissertation project have greatly expanded our understanding of the drivers and long-term impacts of settlement behavior on Madagascar over the past millennium. The analysis of satellite imagery, guided by machine learning and statistical methods, have allowed for a rapid assessment of the island's southwest coast. This has resulted in the documentation of hundreds of new archaeological sites. This new archaeological data provides insight to the driving forces behind human decision making in this region for the last several millennia. Based on this research, we know that social connectivity and community defense were significant contributing factors to the decision of Malagasy communities on where to situate themselves on the landscape. Environmental and climatic contexts, like resource availability and precipitation levels, were also highly influential in people's mobility or settlement decisions. 

 

This project also generated evidence that Malagasy foragers in the Velondriake region developed social organizational networks that were resilient to a slew of environmental and sociopolitical shifts over the past millennium. As such, settlement and mobility strategies among coastal communities has served as an adaptive mechanism to risk posed by climate change, resource availability, and political violence for at least the past 1000 years. This holds important implications for future efforts towards sustainability and resilience in the face of increasing climate related impacts to coastal communities on Madagascar and elsewhere. By integrating traditional methods of mobility-based livelihood strategies into conservation policies, resource use can be better managed in ways that aid biodiversity efforts while minimizing the impact to Malagasy communities who rely on these resources for survival. 

 

In addition to improving our understanding of ancient decision making, this project work has also helped to document the long-lasting and significant impact that ancient foraging populations have made on Madagascar's landscape. Ancient communities altered the vegetation and soil properties throughout much of the study region, which resulted in an increased ability for soil and taxa to retain water in places where people have actively lived for the past several hundred to several thousand years. 

 

Excavations carried out as part of this dissertation uncovered several open-air village sites from the northern, central, and southernmost reaches of the Velondriake area in southwest Madagascar. Charcoal and faunal materials recovered from these sites reveal an extensive use of trees as fuel sources for cooking, marine resource exploitation, and the use of tubers, cacti, and shrubs in dietary contexts. The presence of starvation foods at some excavated areas signifies potential periods of environmental downturn, and these occupations overlap with climatic shifts from very wet conditions (ca. 550 - 450 cal. BP) towards drought conditions (ca. 450 - 300 cal. BP).

 

Excavations also provided the first and only evidence, to date, of stone-tool use in the southwest of Madagascar. A lithic blade recovered from the bottom of one of our excavations likely constitutes an early presence of foragers in the Velondriake region as early as 728 - 1235 years ago. This discovery is especially significant in light of the ongoing debate over when and where humans first arrived on Madagascar. The presence of stone tool use in the southwest adds to an ever-increasing collection of evidence of sustained human occupancy on the island for the past several thousand years. 

 

The findings of this work were shared with local Malagasy communities via a series of public lectures, translated summaries of project findings, and digital models that can be used to plan and conduct archaeological surveys in southwest Madagascar. All work conducted in this project was accomplished in direct collaboration with local communities and local archaeologists, and all findings have been shared in international scientific conferences in addition to peer reviewed scientific publications.

abstractText:
Despite increasing awareness of the critical nature of cybersecurity, the cybersecurity workforce is currently insufficient to meet needs across the public, private, and academic sectors. The project will directly address the growing demand for cybersecurity professionals by increasing the number of effective cybersecurity learning materials available in a standardized and compatible format. These learning materials can then be widely adopted and used in training future members of the cybersecurity workforce. The proposed framework will also incentivize additional cybersecurity scholars to turn their research or teaching materials into case studies. These case studies will be attributable, which will expand societal and community impacts and also positively impact scholars’ research reputations via citations and thus enhance their academic progression.

In this project, the team proposes to develop a simple yet flexible framework named SAGA (Security Arxiv-Github-kAggle), where scholars can easily create cybersecurity case studies related to artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML). For example, these case studies might illustrate the use of machine learning to detect malicious activities in social media or detecting spam/phishing emails using classification. Furthermore, by adopting the notion of “citation” from the academic world and implementing it using three public platforms (arXiv, Github, Kaggle), the SAGA framework allows the developed case studies to be found easily and shared across the cybersecurity community and allows the authors of case studies to be appropriately recognized for their efforts. This attribution is intended to encourage scholars’ participation in creating and sharing such cybersecurity case studies. Finally, the project proposes to evaluate the effectiveness of the developed cybersecurity case studies in improving students’ learning of cybersecurity concepts and skills.

This project is supported by a special initiative of the Secure and Trustworthy Cyberspace (SaTC) program to foster new, previously unexplored, collaborations between the fields of cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, and education. The SaTC program aligns with the Federal Cybersecurity Research and Development Strategic Plan and the National Privacy Research Strategy to protect and preserve the growing social and economic benefits of cyber systems while ensuring security and privacy.

projectOutComesReport:
In this project, we proposed a framework, named SAGA, that enables scholars to easily create cybersecurity case studies—similar to business case studies. More importantly, by adopting the academic notion of citation and operationalizing it through features available on public platforms (e.g., arXiv, GitHub, Kaggle), SAGA allows these case studies to be easily discovered, shared, and reused within the community. It also ensures that the original authors receive proper attribution for their work, thereby encouraging broader participation from scholars in the creation and dissemination of such case studies.

 

Following a literature review in both cybersecurity and human-computer interaction (HCI) domains to examine existing work on the attributable creation of scholarly artifacts, we finalized the design of the SAGA framework, with particular emphasis on defining the essential attributes required for high-quality security case studies. To facilitate seamless dissemination, further, we designed and implemented a prototype interface layer that enables scholars to deposit their case studies directly to GitHub and Kaggle without needing to interact with each platform individually. However, due to limitations in arXiv’s public API that hinder the full realization of SAGA’s capabilities—and in light of novel opportunities presented by the advent of large language models (LLMs)—we expanded the scope of the project to also explore the GenAI-based generation of learning materials and to examine their potential and limitations.

abstractText:
This archaeological project explores the occupation history of the volcanically active Katmai region of the Alaska Peninsula. Archaeological research at two villages abandoned after the massive Novarupta eruption of 1912 will quantify how investments in human, natural, social, economic and built capital affected communities. In a region where the rate of volcanic eruptions in the archaeological record appears to far outpace cultural change, persistent community investments across repeated volcanic events are anticipated to reveal both local and regional strategies for mitigating disaster. Identifying community characteristics that contribute to resiliency has potential to inform planning around current and future hazards. Understanding these past interactions is critical, as climate change and rising sea levels continue to alter lifeways, affect resource access and destroy cultural heritage across the Arctic and Subarctic.

The holistic community capitals framework will be applied to two multicomponent village sites on the Alaska Peninsula. Katmai Village and Savonoski, situated in different environmental zones on either side of a major volcanic epicenter, were occupied until 1912 when they were buried by approximately 60 cm of volcanic ash. Archaeological features at the sites will be identified and mapped using magnetometry, while targeted excavations will recover radiocarbon samples and diagnostic artifacts to produce absolute chronologies. Analysis of lithic and ceramic artifacts, including X-ray fluorescence and neutron activation, will contribute to reconstruction of regional exchange networks. Because Katmai Village and Savonoski continue to hold significant meaning for Alutiit/Sugpiat communities living on the Alaska Peninsula today, project participants will co-design an educational curriculum and experiential program that engages local K-12 students and culture bearers with the archaeological study of their history and heritage.

projectOutComesReport:
This project has enhanced our understanding of how cultures respond to geological hazards in the most volcanically active region on the planet. By compiling a comprehensive radiocarbon record from 1,366 archaeological and geological dates collected on the Alaska Peninsula and Kodiak Island, we produced high-resolution regional chronologies, showing that cultures in this area persisted with minimal disruption from volcanic events. Evidence of the first settlements on the Alaska Peninsula dates back approximately 9,400 years, revealing that locations with the highest diversity of subsistence resources were the most attractive, allowing for uninterrupted habitation.

As plant, animal, and marine species react differently to volcanic events, communities in these productive environments could quickly transition between their primary winter homes and nearby subsistence camps. Our magnetometry surveys of 7,966 m3 across four different archaeological sites uncovered a new site in Katmai Bay with a series of multi-season residential structures occupied for 1,500 years. These surveys also revealed earlier phases of occupation at the Old Savonoski village site and hidden details of structural architecture that show variations in household and community composition and how these changed over time.

Material analyses of stone tools and pottery provided further insights into local adaptive strategies. X-ray fluorescence (XRF) analysis of twelve obsidian artifacts shows that residents obtained stone materials from regions as distant as the Arctic North Slope to the Aleutian Islands, utilizing extensive exchange networks that spanned nearly 1,000 kilometers in either direction. In contrast, a different pattern emerged from the analysis of 82 basalt tools, indicating a stronger preference for diversifying tool materials rather than relying on a specific local source.

Moreover, our Neutron Activation Analyses (NAA) of 99 pottery samples suggest that this significant technological advancement may have originated from newcomers to the region. Later, immigrants introduced different styles and techniques that locals adopted as they continued to utilize their familiar clay sources. The patterns of cultural change on the Alaska Peninsula indicate a trend toward increasing populations and expanding social networks, resulting in a cultural system. The long-standing tradition of maintaining secondary subsistence camps allowed large villages to thrive and grow near the sources of these volcanic events.

Following this long-standing pattern, even those communities affected by the massive 1912 Novarupta volcanic event escaped sans substantial injuries by using familiar travel routes to evacuate to shelter in neighboring communities. This time, however, the fumaroles of the Valley of Ten Thousand Smokes steamed ominously for over a decade, and shifting ash deposits threatened catastrophic landslides. Nevertheless, descendants of the communities that relocated following the Novarupta eruption still experience a strong connection to their ancestral home.

There is little evidence to suggest that the pre-contact inhabitants of the Alaska Peninsula were unfamiliar with or unprepared for the risk of volcanic eruptions. Instead of viewing the landscape around the Katmai volcano cluster as dangerous and worthy of abandonment, a more fitting perspective is that the area's first settlers maintained a strong attachment to Katmai through both prosperous and challenging times. The minerals released by minor volcanic events likely provided a nutrient boost contributing to high ecosystem productivity and abundant subsistence yields. These benefits encouraged new migrations into the area, particularly during the late pre-contact period. In contrast, more significant eruptions may have stretched available resources to their limits and hindered community growth.

This award provides support to U.S. researchers participating in a project competitively selected by a 55-country initiative on global change research through the Belmont Forum.  The Belmont Forum is a consortium of research funding organizations focused on support for transdisciplinary approaches to global environmental change challenges and opportunities.  It aims to accelerate delivery of the international research most urgently needed to remove critical barriers to sustainability by aligning and mobilizing international resources. Each partner country provides funding for their researchers within a consortium to alleviate the need for funds to cross international borders. This approach facilitates effective leveraging of national resources to support excellent research on topics of global relevance best tackled through a multinational approach, recognizing that global challenges need global solutions. This award provides support for the U.S. researchers to cooperate in consortia that consist of partners from at least three of the participating countries to address the growing need for assessment and reduction of disaster risk, collaborative co-design of resilience strategies with a breadth of stakeholders, and scientifically and technologically enhanced responses to disasters.  

This project seeks to enhance the resilience of low-income communities living in disaster prone areas. The focus is on low-lying coastal zones that have high risks of droughts and floods in selected parts of Brazil, East Africa and North America. It develops the geographic and socio-economic knowledge of persons living in economically depressed and riverbed areas by gathering georeferenced data on infrastructures and natural heritage of potential sites. The project team will use machine learning and big data analytical approaches to identify optimal disaster resilient-housing urban design and planning packages considering projected climate change related extreme weather scenarios until 2050.  The project will investigate potential barriers to technology adoption through designing and prototyping an affordable, disaster-resilient, low-income housing system that use sustainable locally resourced materials.

projectOutComesReport:
A key research question that underpinned the work here was - What resilience measures may be valuable in terms of reduction of potential loss & damage plus reduced future risk? Exploring this question holistically requires input from several disciplines - climate science, building design, material sciences, urban planning, social sciences, and health sciences. Extreme weather events pose the greatest threat to the aging housing stock. During the completed stakeholder engagement events, there was consensus that resilience depends on the ability to anticipate, absorb, adapt to, and/or rapidly recover from a potentially disruptive event. Reliance on hard engineering and infrastructure solutions alone cannot solve this problem. The research has integrated the roles of human, social, and natural capital in reducing vulnerability and increasing resilience of low incoming housing in diverse contexts. These findings can inform revisions to building codes and land use planning e.g. zoning to promote the deployment of nature-based systems for flood water management. We have identified co-benefits that can help converge efforts that are being advanced by built environment, earth scientists, health sciences and data sciences. 

The disruption of the supply chains during the pandemic in 2020 increased our appreciation of the value of locally resourced materials. We have demonstrated at the laboratory scale that cold sintering approach can produce high quality bricks that have strength properties equivalent to fired bricks. Bricks are an integral part of building envelopes around the world. These bricks are produced through energy inefficient processes. For example, commonly used bricks are usually fired at between 900 and 1000 degrees Celsius. As part of previous research efforts, we have sought to address this problem through investigating the use of unfired compressed earth bricks. One of the challenges associated with the production of compressed earth bricks is the scale of production. In this current research, we are exploring the feasibility and viability of using the Cold Sintering Process to produce high quality bricks at room temperature.  The input material is Calcium Silicate (CaSiO3). Our findings demonstrate that the CSP could yield sustainable and resilient masonry units. In subsequent efforts, we explore the use of a broader variety of locally available materials.

Based on input and feedback from several non-academic stakeholders, we have developed a framework for a data, information and knowledge management warehouse that can be used to enhance the resilience of low-income housing. The proposed platform will integrate content from heterogenous sources. Various stakeholders can access content tailored to their needs and requirements.  This enables prompt decision making and action. For example, occupants of structures identified to be at risk would access content on affordable building renovation solutions. Humanitarian actors can extract information that simplifies the process of developing response strategies that are aligned with the needs, capabilities, and priorities of a specific community. The proposed warehouse can also help policy makers to be more transparent with respect to resource allocation priorities for shelter deployment and reconstruction. Built environment researchers and practitioners can derive information that can be used to inform the development or modification of, for example, design manual building standards and codes. Information flow among the stakeholders enhances collaborative approach to disaster management while also allowing them to contribute to the platform based on their experiences in disaster management and response.

The analysis that has been done on the data collected from households was directed at identifying and implementing non-linear causal methodologies that can potentially better explain the statistical significance of the building envelope and the immediate health impact after flood events. Machine learning tools, such as clustering, were selected as an initial methodology to determine if it could reveal higher statistical significance compared to statistical analysis of individual variables.

abstractText:
Millions of youth participate in out-of-school (OS) programs each year. Hispanic and Black youth participate at twice the rate of Caucasian youth in OS programs, making OS programs promising venues for addressing inequities in STEM. Although a majority of programs offer STEM experiences, less than a third of OS STEM programming includes engineering. High-quality curricular materials can support the introduction of engineering into these environments. However, such resources need to be carefully designed to provide learning opportunities that ensure all youth can participate, contribute, and benefit. One of the most rapidly growing populations in the U.S. at the elementary level are English learners (ELs). These youth face the challenge of simultaneously learning English and academic content, such as engineering. Few, if any, engineering curricula exist for OS settings that include scaffolds for ELs and their educators. The Youth Engineering Solutions: Engineering Opportunities in Out-of-School Programs for English Learners (YES-OS) project will refine a set of equity-oriented design principles for OS engineering that are informed by strategies for ELs. It will work closely with OS educators and stakeholders to develop and study two OS engineering curricular units for youth ages 9–12. Units will feature socially engaged, real-world design challenges, engage youth in engineering practices, and provide language scaffolds. The educative materials will include youth, educator, and family-facing resources and will be designed to scale nationwide. Research will study how curricula can provide opportunities for ELs and support educators. YES-OS’s principles, resources, and research will inform asset-based models that build on youth’s experience to create more equitable educational opportunities and thus broaden participation in engineering.

YES-OS will investigate ways that equity-oriented OS engineering curricula provide opportunities for ELs to learn knowledge, discourses, and practices; bring their cultures, experiences, and ideas to the engineering projects; expand their repertoire of identities and interests; and enhance membership in the learning community. The project will: (1) refine, apply, study, and modify a set of equity-oriented design principles for OS engineering curricula that are informed by strategies for ELs, (2) develop, test, and revise two OS engineering units for youth in ages 9–12 that instantiate the principles using design-based research, (3) begin to examine affordances of engineering for ELs in OS programming. This will include investigating how the engineering units engage youth in disciplinary knowledge and practices, scaffold social and academic discourses, increase interest in STEM, and foster a community that supports participation and identity development, and (4) explore how equity-based engineering curricula can support OS educators as they build their knowledge of and confidence with engineering, engineering practices, and ELs and create asset-based engineering programming. YES-OS will use design-based research to systematically design curriculum while simultaneously researching the efficacy of the curriculum design and the learning environments they foster. Thirty OS educators nationwide will work with developers to test frameworks and materials. Data including educator feedback, youth work, surveys, lesson observations and video, and focus groups will be analyzed using multiple qualitative and quantitative methods. Resources and findings will be disseminated to educators, stakeholders, the public, and researchers through websites, conferences, webinars, newsletters, research articles, and social media.

abstractText:
The broader impact/commerical potential of this I-Corps project involves the use of brochosome-inspired coatings for optical, energy, and sustainability applications. Brochosomes are intricately structured microscopic granules secreted by insects and typically found on their body surface.  The proposed brochosome-inspired coating technology could be integrated into camera or sensing devices to suppress stray reflections and to further enhance the sensor sensitivity. In addition, the brochosome-inspired coating could be engineered and incorporated onto solar panels to enhance optical transmission to improve solar energy harvesting. The antireflective coating could also be applied onto glass and window surfaces to improve energy efficiency of buildings, in addition to serving as a bird-friendly coating to reduce bird collisions for environmental sustainability. 

This I-Corps project is based on a brochosome-inspired optical coating characterized by three-dimensional, hierarchical micro- and nanostructures to suppress reflection from ultraviolet to near-infrared light at different incident angles. The proposed technology has demonstrated that brochosome-inspired coatings can be applied onto various surfaces and can prevent reflection of ultraviolet to near infrared light by as much as ~99%. The antireflective performances of the brochosomes-inspired coating can be tailored by engineering the geometries of the micro- and nanostructures suitable for various optical applications.

projectOutComesReport:
Intellectual Merit: The objective of this NSF I-Corps project is to conduct market feasibility research and customer discovery to identify the potential markets and commercialization partners for synthetic brochosomes. These synthetic brochosomes are biologically inspired micro- and nanoscale granules mimicking the intricate buckyball structure of the natural brochosomes produced by leafhoppers. Through the NSF I-Corps program, the team successfully conducted 101 interviews with customers interested in various applications, including bird-friendly glass, solar-panel coatings, paints, cosmetics, and medical devices. Importantly, the team has identified significant potential markets in solar-panel coatings, cosmetics, defense coatings, and medical devices. In addition, the team has also explored the potential of distributing synthetic brochosomes through a global chemical and materials supplier. Discussions revolved around manufacturing strategies, considering options such as in-house production or licensing to a third-party manufacturer for distribution through the distributor.

Broader Impact: The participating team has learned the scientific process of building a startup and developing a business model using a business model canvas. The process enabled the team to formulate a specific plan for the commercialization of their product. The program has provided training to a faculty member, a graduate student, and an undergraduate student on the essential steps to build a viable business. Following their participation in the I-Corps program, the undergraduate student was recruited by a Penn State spinoff company to continue his startup journey, and the graduate student was awarded the Diefenderfer Graduate Fellowship to further support her entrepreneurship development. The faculty member has also continued to seek additional support to advance the development of scalable manufacturing of synthetic brochosomes for those high-value applications identified in this program.

abstractText:
Natural history collections record the world’s diversity through time and support the scientific community’s understanding of changing ecosystem dynamics. In the face of declining insect biodiversity worldwide, it is more important now than ever for entomology collections to preserve, digitize, and disseminate specimen data to the broader community. The Frost Entomological Museum at Penn State cares for more than 1.3 million specimens that span the diversity of insects. This collection stands to grow further, through the incorporation of satellite collections of pollinators, especially bees (more than 125,000 specimens), and through the activities of the Insect Biodiversity Center (IBC), a recently established research initiative at Penn State. The infrastructure provided through this grant increases the storage capacity of the Frost by 50%, allowing for the curation of these collections and to serve as a repository for scaled up efforts to understand insect diversity through time. The award also provides the resources to digitize the substantial aphid collection (approximately 224,000 specimens on 49,000 slides), which holds important data regarding these insects’ plant hosts, and aquatic insects (approximately 100,000 specimens in 15,000 vials), which are indicators of habitat health. These improvements will facilitate research that addresses native pollinator decline, epidemiology, global climate change and its impact on species distributions and invasive species, niche restrictions, indicator species, and the evolutionary history of insects. The project will also generate data that contribute to ongoing research on imperiled insects and will fill critical taxonomic, geographical, and temporal gaps in existing datasets.

A high-density compactor storage system will be installed in the Frost Museum in order to accommodate new rows of cabinets for pinned insects. These cabinets will accommodate approximately 1,600 drawers of expanded space. A portion of this storage will be utilized by incorporating the pollinator collection previously housed at Penn State’s Fruit Research and Extension Center and specimens generated by Penn State’s Center for Pollinator Research. The aphid collection, which consists of slide-mounted specimens, will be imaged on a flatbed scanner and then moved to new custom-built slide cabinets. The slide scans will be transcribed in the Frost Museum database, georeferenced, and the data shared with iDigBio and the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF). The aquatic insect collection likewise will be imaged and rehoused in new, expanded ethanol storage. The lot images will be transcribed, georeferenced, and the data shared with the above repositories, making them accessible to the public. A graduate student and at least two undergraduates will receive training in collections care, management, and digitization.

projectOutComesReport:
This museum infrastructure project accomplished three critical objectives, solidifying the Frost Entomological Museum at Penn State as a stable, long-term resource for biodiversity science. First, the project expanded museum storage capacity by over 50% through the installation of new, American-made collection furniture and containers designed to house the museum's growing collection of arthropod specimens from biotic surveys. Second, the team reorganized, digitized, and rehoused a world-class aphid collection containing more than 250,000 specimens, creating a comprehensive resource for future research on these economically significant plant-feeding insects. Third, the project encompassed the imaging, digitization, and rehousing of an extensive aquatic insect collection to support studies of species that provide critical ecosystem services and serve as vital indicators of habitat health. Upon completion, the project had contributed more than 5,000 new aquatic insect records to major biodiversity data portals (Ecdysis.org and GBIF.org), with thousands of additional specimens prepared for continued digitization beyond the funding period. The grant established sustainable digitization workflows that will continue indefinitely through the dedicated efforts of interns and volunteers.

The intellectual merits of this project cover a broad spectrum of opportunities for knowledge expansion and for the exploration of  creative and potentially transformative concepts. Collection digitization opens these resources to scientists from around the world, for research in multiple domains: niche modeling, systematics, ecology, host-parasite dynamics, invasion biology, biological control, etc. This process also increases awareness and accessibility of a rich resource, with latent potential. By the end of the project, more than 500 outside research projects had used data generated by the Frost Entomological Museum, as measured by citations at the Global Biodiversity Information Facility. By securing historical specimens in archival containers, protected from agents of deterioration (high humidity, temperature fluctuations, water intrusion, museum pests, etc.), Frost Museum staff have ensured that future research on this material remains maximally feasible. 

The broader impacts of this project likewise are multi-faceted, and they will continue long after the funding period. The newly digitized and reorganized collections have been used for enhanced STEM education and public engagement, for example, in displays and interactive exercises. At least eight project members received training in natural history collections management, including specimen handling, digitization, and the informatics associated with data sharing. Hundreds of university and high school students learned about collections science, during multiple engagement events and class visits during the project. Thousands of museum visitors learned about natural history collections - their development and myriad uses - and arthropod biology more generally, through exhibits that focused on and was facilitated by this infrastructure grant.

abstractText:
Wiring light on a chip like electronic circuits, integrated photonics provides a promising long-term solution for increasing demands for data transmission bandwidth and energy efficiency of computing and communication systems. A photonic integrated circuit (PIC) combining many light-controlling components into a single chip, similar to complementary metal oxide semiconductor (CMOS) chips that have revolutionized the electronics industry, offers great advantages in terms of speed, bandwidth, reliability, scalability, power consumption, and etc. In order to fully exploit the benefits of PICs in free-space applications, it is crucial to have an interface that can flexibly control light when it converts between guided and free-space modes. However, conventional coupling techniques such as edge couplers and surface gratings have limited functionalities and lack of the capability to complete control over light. Although arrays of gratings can achieve more advanced functions, such as off-chip beam steering, focusing, and holographic image construction, they have large footprints and suffer from loss due to the existence of high-order diffractions. Therefore, there is a strong demand for a unified approach to achieve complex free-space optical functions on PICs. The major goal of the proposed program is to develop a hybrid architecture where metasurfaces – ultrathin artificial surfaces which manipulate light by locally imposing abrupt changes to optical properties through engineered sub-wavelength structures also known as meta-atoms – are directly driven by guided waves to realize complex free-space functions. The proposed program will include closely integrated educational activities (such as developing a new course on nanophotonics) designed to stimulate undergraduate and graduate students to pursue engineering career by exposing them to the exciting development of nanophotonic devices solving important societal problems in optical computing, communication, and networking. Besides, nanophotonic cloud computing tools will be developed that are free-to-run in web browsers without the need for powerful workstations that will be especially beneficial for economically disadvantaged research communities worldwide. Furthermore, outreach activities, such as organizing fun exhibitions of optics effects, will also be provided to promote the interests and participations of K-12 teachers and students in local schools and public libraries.


The overarching goal of this research program is to combine two powerful, complimentary technologies – the integrated photonics and the metasurface – together to develop a new architecture where metasurfaces are directly driven by the guided waves in PICs for realizing complex optical functions. The meta-atom building blocks with sizes much smaller than the optical wavelength will be placed on top of photonic integrated components. Through the metasurfaces consisting of such meta-atoms, the guided light can be molded to any desired complex light fields in free space or in PICs. The proposed research will establish a theory, design, material synthesis, and device nanofabrication platform and provide a complete photonic integrated route for complete light control. Tremendous benefits will be offered by the proposed hybrid architecture: (1) metasurfaces that are driven directly by guided waves in PICs; (2) light can be routed to different metasurfaces performing multiple complex functions on a single waveguide; and (3) PICs are now empowered with the ability to control light at the subwavelength scale. The technology will pave new exciting ways for building multifunctional photonic integrated devices with flexible access to free space and lead to a large spectrum of novel applications particularly where the grand challenges of the system size, weight, and power, performance are concerned.

abstractText:
In today's globalized world, people increasingly encounter speakers with a foreign accent: the majority of English speakers across the world, for example, are non-native speakers. Moreover, natural speech communication rarely takes place in ideal listening conditions and we often listen to others when surrounded by background noise. Processing and comprehending foreign-accented speech in noisy backgrounds has thus become a common characteristic of everyday communication. This is also true for school-aged children, as their peers may be foreign-accented speakers and their classrooms can be noisy. Prior linguistic research has demonstrated that the addition of background noise can impact the understanding of foreign-accented speech, more so than native-accented speech, and increased cognitive demand has been proposed as the possible explanation. 

This project measures cognitive demands during sentence processing, combining behavioral and neurocognitive (EEG) techniques, to examine three questions: What are the linguistic-cognitive mechanisms underlying the processing of foreign-accented and native-accented sentences embedded in background noise and in quiet conditions in (1) adults and (2) children? (3) What are potential sources of individual variability in behavioral and neural responses to semantic anomalies in native- and foreign-accented sentences presented in background noise and in quiet? Two age groups will be tested in two experiments: young adults and children aged 9-11. In the EEG task, participants listen to native- and foreign-accented English sentences. Half the sentences in each accent condition will be embedded in background noise, and the remaining sentences in quiet; half the sentences will contain semantic anomalies and half will be semantically well-formed. Participants will also complete a language background questionnaire, reporting demographic information, language use, proficiency, and accent exposure, as well as behavioral tasks measuring individual differences in linguistic and cognitive abilities. This project provides foundational insights on the cognitive and neural bases of foreign- and native-accented speech processing in noisy and quiet environments. The outcomes also have real-life implications and can, for example, inform educators on facilitating optimal learning environments in their classrooms.

projectOutComesReport:
As the majority of English speakers across the world are non-native speakers who often speak with an accent, we increasingly encounter speakers with a nonnative accent in today’s globalized world. Moreover, we often listen to others when surrounded by background noise, as natural speech communication rarely takes place in ideal listening conditions. Processing and comprehending nonnative-accented speech in noisy backgrounds has thus become a common characteristic of everyday communication. This is also true for school-aged children, as their peers may be nonnative-accented speakers and their classrooms can be noisy. What are the consequences of understanding native- and nonnative-accented speech in noisy conditions, for example when surrounded by other speakers in a noisy restaurant or a classroom? This project measured cognitive demands during spoken sentence processing, combining behavioral and neurocognitive (EEG) techniques, to examine the following main question: What are the linguistic-cognitive mechanisms underlying the processing of nonnative-accented and native-accented sentences embedded in background noise and presented in quiet conditions, in adults and children?

Two groups of monolingual speakers of American English were tested: young adults (Study 1; n=36) and children aged 9-12 (Study 2; n=43). All participants listened to American-accented and Chinese-accented English sentences. Half the sentences in each accent condition were embedded in background noise (multi-talker babble), and the other half of the sentences were presented in quiet. While participants listened to the sentence, their brain activity was recorded using EEG (measuring Event-Related Potentials and neural oscillations). After each sentence, participants repeated to sentence back to measure their sentence comprehension (verbal repetition accuracy). Participants also completed a language background questionnaire, reporting demographic information, their language use, proficiency, and accent exposure, as well as behavioral tasks measuring individual differences in linguistic and cognitive abilities.

The verbal repetition accuracy scores of the adults showed that they were more accurate repeating back native-accented (86.96%) than nonnative-accented sentences (67.18%) and sentences presented in quiet (88.29%) than in noise (65.85%). Even though children’s verbal accuracy was generally lower than that of adults, their performance aligned with that of adults: children were more accurate when repeating back native-accented (77.86%) versus nonnative-accented sentences (49.22%) and sentences presented in quiet (78.57%) versus noise (45.52%).

For the neural data, we employed the frequently used semantic violation paradigm that presents sentences with or without an odd word (a semantic anomaly) and measures the brain’s capacity to detect the semantic errors (eliciting the N400 ERP component that reflects how well listeners can access the meaning of the word while listening to the sentence). The neural data of the adult listeners showed that native-accented sentences in the quiet condition elicited the largest N400 effect, followed by native-accented sentences in noise, which in turn elicited a larger N400 than nonnative-accented sentences in quiet. Lastly, nonnative-accented sentences in noise did not modulate the N400, suggesting that semantic access is particularly challenging when listening to nonnative accented speech embedded in background noise.

With respect to the neural data, children’s performance was comparable to that of adults. Child listeners showed the largest N400 effect for native-accented sentences presented in quiet, followed by the native-accented sentences in noise and the nonnative-accented sentences in quiet. Nonnative-accented sentences presented in background noise did not elicit an N400 effect. These data indicate that accessing the meaning of words is easiest for native speech presented in quiet and becomes more challenging when speech is embedded in background noise. For both adults (Study 1) and children (Study 2), the ERP data were supported by additional measures of brain activity (i.e. time frequency analyses and power changes in the alpha and theta frequency bands).

The combined behavioral and neural data of Study 1 (adults) and Study 2 (children) align with theoretical models of speech processing that propose that as the distance between the speech signal and the listener’s phonological representations (based on their native language) increases, understanding the meaning of words while listening to sentences relies more heavily on top-down processing and requires greater allocation of cognitive resources. One of the practical implications of this study is that a noisy classroom environment will impede children’s speech comprehension, even more strongly so when listening to nonnative-accented speech.

This research project provided hands-on training to nine undergraduate students and one graduate student. The undergraduate trainees were involved in stimulus creation and task development and were also trained in collecting, analyzing, and interpreting behavioral and neural data. The graduate student was also trained on experimental methods in addition to professional development skills, such as academic job applications and networking; paper writing and revising; dissemination of research findings to academic and non-academic audiences; science communication; mentoring (under)graduate students; manuscript reviewing; and grant writing.

abstractText:
This project will advance the state-of-the-art in cross-disciplinary areas including motion signal processing, machine learning (ML), sign language modeling, and real-time ML with dynamic device/edge partitioning, to develop new technology for automatic Sign Language Recognition (SLR) and translation to spoken language that enables  more seamless communication between deaf and hearing people. The technology will incorporate wearable devices (such as a smartwatch, smart ring, and earphones) that are gaining in popularity, and will have broad impact through its introduction in deaf communities along with a sign language equivalent of voice assistants such as Amazon Alexa. The project will establish a pipeline of collaboration with deaf students, as well as courses based on SLR technology that will be disseminated through MOOC platforms such as Coursera. Additional impact will derive from workshops on wearable computing that will be conducted at the K-12 level, and a "sign-to-speech" library that will be publicly released for extensibility of the new technology to multiple sign languages. 

To achieve its goals this research will include three thrusts: Development of ML models with efficient training that can perform accurate SLR by fusing multimodal input data from wearable devices that capture body motion and facial expressions; Implementation of efficient ML models by means of optimal partitioning between end-device and edge resources to achieve the best tradeoff in real time performance and SLR accuracy; Design of systematic user studies with fluent sign language users both for generating training data for ML models as well as for validation of accuracy, usability, and acceptability of the technology within the deaf community.

abstractText:
Proposal Number: 2042154
Principal Investigator: Saptarshi Das
Title: CAREER: Two-Dimensional Straintronic Field Effect Transistor
Institution: Pennsylvania State Univ University Park

Nontechnical Abstract:
Energy efficient computing will revolutionize next generations of smart and secure electronic devices, and benefit all sectors of modern society including agriculture, healthcare, automation, communication, defense, and infrastructure. In fact, the 21st century, which promises to thrive on big data, remote sensing, Internet-of-Things (IoT) and so on, demands novel devices, which can operate with power so frugal that ambient energy harvesting may accommodate all of their needs. The conventional silicon based complementary metal oxide semiconductor technology is inadequate for achieving such goals necessitating novel material discovery and device level innovations. This may be achieved in two-dimensional straintronic field effect transistors by utilizing a unique property of two-dimensional materials, namely, strain induced dynamic bandgap engineering and integrating it with piezoelectric nanotransducers, which will be explored in the proposed research. 

Technical Abstract
The aim of the proposal is to experimentally demonstrate steep slope switching in two-dimensional straintronic field effect transistors (2D SFET) exploiting in-operando and uniaxial strain engineering in 2D transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs). The 2D SFET can defy the thermodynamic limit imposed by Boltzmann statistics in conventional metal oxide semiconductor field effect transistors (FET) and achieve sub-60mV/decade subthreshold swing at room temperature along with high on-state performance. Realization of 2D SFET requires monolithic integration of 2D TMDC based FETs with piezoelectric (PE) ceramic based nanotransducers. The PE expands in response to an applied gate bias and transduces an out-of-plane stress on the 2D channel material reducing its bandgap. The result is an internal voltage amplification that leads to steep slope switching. While static, in-plane, and biaxial strain is used in conventional silicon technology, dynamic strain engineering is a relatively uncharted territory. Consequently, exploration of novel straintronic devices based on novel 2D TMDCs will add new fundamental knowledge towards advancing concepts for resolving critical computing needs and grand engineering challenges. Furthermore, the proposed straintronic platform will offer exciting opportunities to develop novel concepts including straintronic neuromorphic devices (SNDs) for brain-inspired computing, straintronic memory devices (SMDs) for in-memory computing, and straintronic security devices (SSDs) for secure computing.

projectOutComesReport:
Modern society increasingly relies on computing technologies for communication, artificial intelligence, data analytics, and sensing. However, conventional silicon-based electronics are approaching fundamental physical limits, creating an urgent need for new materials and device concepts that can enable more energy-efficient and scalable computing technologies. This project explored the use of two-dimensional (2D) materials, which are atomically thin semiconductors, to develop new types of electronic devices and computing systems.

A central focus of the project was the development of straintronic devices, where mechanical strain is used to control electronic behavior in atomically thin materials. The research demonstrated that strain can be used to create extremely sharp switching in electronic devices by mechanically controlling nanoscale contacts. In particular, we developed graphene- and MoTe₂-based devices in which applied strain produces nanoscale cracking and reconnection of metal contacts, leading to very abrupt transitions between ON and OFF states. This mechanism enables switching behavior that can surpass the limits of conventional silicon transistors, offering a promising pathway toward ultra-low-power electronics.

Beyond individual device demonstrations, the project also advanced the broader field of two-dimensional nanoelectronics. The team developed new strategies for building high-performance transistors using materials such as MoS₂ and WSe₂ and demonstrated complementary transistor technologies that can be used to construct logic circuits. The research further explored how devices based on atomically thin materials can be integrated into monolithic three-dimensional (3D) electronic systems, where multiple layers of devices are stacked vertically to enable more compact and powerful computing architectures.

The project also investigated emerging computing approaches enabled by these materials, including neuromorphic and in-memory computing, which are inspired by the way the human brain processes information. These technologies aim to significantly reduce the energy required for data processing and artificial intelligence applications.

The outcomes of the project have been disseminated widely through publications in leading peer-reviewed journals and presentations at major international conferences. The research has contributed to advancing the broader field of nanoelectronics by demonstrating how atomically thin materials can be used not only for fundamental device studies but also for functional electronic and computing systems.

The project also had a strong impact on education and workforce development. Thirteen PhD students were supported and successfully graduated through this effort. These students received interdisciplinary training in nanofabrication, materials science, device physics, and advanced computing technologies. Many have gone on to careers in the semiconductor industry or postdoctoral research positions, helping to build the highly skilled workforce needed for future electronics innovation.

Overall, this project established new scientific foundations for strain-controlled electronic devices and two-dimensional nanoelectronics, while demonstrating pathways toward future energy-efficient computing technologies that could help address the growing global demand for information processing.

abstractText:
Vaccination is the most effective method to prevent infectious diseases like coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) and prompt herd immunity. However,  herd immunity could be slowed or stalled if people hesitated to be vaccinated. This project aims to facilitate informed vaccination decisions. The research aims to illuminate how people’s vaccination decisions evolve in response to their social context. The project’s novelty is to follow participants over time to evaluate their real-world decision making about vaccination. The project will advance the state-of-the-art on risk communication during crises and decision-making under uncertainty. The project will identify effective communication about COVID-19 vaccines that are understandable by, and applicable to, the public. The project could ultimately improve the immunization rate of the population to pass the threshold for herd immunity and the collective health benefits of immunization. 

The project entails four tasks that will advance the understanding of human vaccination decision-making under risk and uncertainty. (1 ) Develop communications about the COVID-19 vaccines that are experimentally varied in completeness, transparency, and correctness by leveraging the standards of risk communication in the health domain.  (2) Evaluate the effectiveness of proposed communications in enhancing people’s knowledge of COVID-19 vaccines and informing their vaccination decisions.  (3) Examine the effectiveness of proposed communications on informing peoples’ vaccination decisions in real-world application settings. (4) Investigate how people respond to uncertainties of different situations in order to understand how vaccination decisions evolve throughout the current vaccination campaign.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

projectOutComesReport:
Evidence-based information on the benefits and risks of vaccines is necessary for informed vaccination decision-making. Leveraging the standards of good risk communication, we proposed evidence-based, transparent (benefits and risks) communication of COVID-19 vaccines. With the emerging variants of SARS-CoV-2, we further explore factors that are critical for human’s acceptance of a booster does of COVID-19 vaccines. The online studies with representative samples showed that transparent and evidence-based communication can be effective in mitigating people’s vaccine hesitancy.  Moreover, such communication can increase people’s COVID-19 (continuous) vaccination intention and confidence.  Such communication was even more effective for the unvaccinated group compared to the vaccinated group. Evidence-based communication was effective in helping people comprehend the safety of COVID-19 vaccines. 

A few works have further investigated human’s trust in XAI for misinformation mitigation (e.g., Seo et la., 2019; Epstein et al., 2022). In agreement with prior work, our current study replicated previous findings in a novel context (i.e., COVID-19 misinformation). Moreover, we identified other critical factors of XAI (e.g., the framing effect and the impact of system reliability) for human misinformation detection and mitigation. In general, this line of work is one of the pioneering studies in the space of XAI for misinformation detection and mitigation, which has the potential to inspire new research directions in the community. 

We have also explored the COVID-19 misinformation in deepfake contexts. This is one of the first works to caution against the impact of deepfake in the downstream tasks, which could guide the design and training of human deepfake detection and mitigation. 

During the COVID-19 pandemic, the pandemic tracking app has been shown as a valuable tool to understand how humans perceive and manage privacy and utility in the context of sensitive personal data.  Moreover, individuals have diverse values and varied privacy preferences.  With directly interacting with the users, our study revealed the dynamics of user privacy preferences when deploying privacy-enhancing technologies, which can be used to enhance the state-of-the-art technical solutions (e.g., sampling and scaling mechanism for individualized DP). 

We train graduate students (two female) to work in interdisciplinary teams and conduct research in information science.

abstractText:
The goal of this project is to obtain a photosynthetic bioproduction platform that can efficiently convert sunlight and CO2 into bioproducts of interest, through iterative removal of selected genes from a cyanobacterium.  Cyanobacteria are oxygenic photosynthetic prokaryotes that are uniquely poised to become optimal platforms for sustainable bioproduction using sunlight and atmospheric CO2 as well as free and ubiquitous substrates. The genes selected for removal would be identified with the aid of computational methods and gene editing techniques. Gene removal is accomplished without compromising the growth rate of the organism. This project trains several national and international undergraduate students under different collaborative programs, in the design and implementation of molecular tools, relevant computational techniques and physiology of photosynthetic organisms. In addition, the project is designed to align with a variety of scientific entrepreneurial ventures. 

This project develops Synechococcus 2973, a cyanobacterium displaying the fastest photoautotrophic growth ever observed, into an ideal chassis strain by streamlining its genome in a multi-step process that involves state-of-the-art genome-editing technology, guided by experimental analysis and metabolic modeling. Efficacy of reduction is assessed by both growth rate and productivity of a plug-in reporter pathway. Minimizing the genome while retaining fast growth eases the metabolic burden on the strain, removes cryptic regulatory processes that challenge predictable engineering, and improves understanding and control over this powerful autotrophic workhorse. The creation of a novel streamlined model cyanobacterium is a significant step in achieving an industrial “green E. coli” and establishing the foundation for a sustainable bioeconomy.

This award is co-funded by the Systems and Synthetic Biology Cluster in the Division of Molecular and Cellular Biosciences and the Cellular and Biochemical Engineering Program in the Division of Chemical, Bioengineering, Environmental and Transport Systems.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

jrnl.auth: Sengupta, Annesha and Bandyopadhyay, Anindita and Sarkar, Debolina and Hendry, John I. and Schubert, Max G. and Liu, Deng and Church, George M. and Maranas, Costas D. and Pakrasi, Himadri B.

program: NANOSCALE BIO CORE
projectOutComesReport:
This effort aimed to integrate computations and experiments to come up with ways to streamline genomic regions which are dispensable for biotechnological application of cyanobacterial strains. The key idea was that by reducing the costs of transcription and translation cellular resources could be diverted towards faster growth and bioproduction goals. To this end, we developed and implemented the software tool minGenome that identifies the largest available contiguous stretch of DNA that can be removed as it does not encode for any required functions under the controlled conditions in a bioreactor. The tool identifies a ranked list the longest, second longest, etc. stretch of DNA that can be deleted.   Application of minGenome to Synechococcus elongatus UTEX 2973 identified regions that can be deleted. Experimental testing confirmed that the predictions led to improved growth characteristics. To further boost productivity, we also computationally explored and experimentally added sugar transporters that would further boost carbon uptake by leveraging ATP synthesis generated through photosynthesis. Computational analysis identified the flux maps associated with this new source of carbon and the associated ATP costs. Streamlined strains with sugar importers were created and tested confirming the hypothesized gains. Finally, our team developed an updated open-source software tool to support flux elucidation for cyano systems allowing for the convenient integration of 13C, 2H and 15N tracer information for flux elucidation.   Overall, the work perfumed in this project leveraged an iterative process using state-of-the-art genome-editing technology guided by experimental analysis and computational tools.

abstractText:
Abstract

This project studies how differences in firms' beliefs about project feasibility, success and future potential profits affect research and development (R&D) activity. These differences may arise due to firms’ prior experience with similar projects or how farther along a firm is in R&D process. Firms have an incentive to learn what their rivals know. While learning about rivals’ progress may be easier in some industries such as pharmaceuticals due to reporting regulations, it is challenging in other industries as firms protect their R&D specific information.  The project is centered around three major research questions. First, the project explores firm incentives to share private information with others and its impact on the society. Second, the research examines whether firms should make R&D progress public or not. Third, the project looks at the reasons behind why startups focus on radical innovations and new products whereas established firms tend to pursue incremental innovations and improvements to existing products. The project has policy and regulatory implications in understanding the role of information asymmetry and information sharing on R&D activities for startups and established firms.

This research focuses on R&D races where rivals have asymmetric information about the feasibility of the project. The project explores three issues. First, if firms can commit to be truthful, then the benefits of better information to a firm seem to outweigh competitive concerns. Although firms should have an incentive to share what they know, this decreases the probability of success and is detrimental from a social perspective. Second, firms can invest more in R&D if they do not share R&D progress publicly as information on a rival abandoning a line of research has a strong discouragement effect on others. Third, the observed regularity about incremental and radical innovations can be explained in terms of information: Smaller startup firms can usually observe the R&D activity of larger, established firms better than the other way around, which affects risk taking behavior. This project studies these issues in a rich setting incorporating imperfect monitoring of R&D activity by firms, capital constraints and intellectual capital. projectOutComesReport:
The major findings of the project entitled "Innovation and Information" and the are summarized below.

R&D Races. In our paper, "Startups and Upstarts," (Journal of Political Economy, 2021) Awaya and I studied competition between an established firm and startup to develop a new drur, say. The firms are equally adept at R&D but because of its experience, the established firm has a better idea whether the research is likely to be successful or not. This better understanding of the feasibility of the project is the only asymmetry between the two firms. We show that despite this disadvantage, the startup is more likely to succeed than the established firm. The channel by which better information becomes a competitive disadvantage stems from the fact that better information dulls the incentive to learn from one's rival. The startup is willing to learn from the established firm; the reverse does not hold.

Panic Buying. Awaya and I began work on our paper "Panics and Prices," (Journal of Economic Theory, 2024) during the Covid epidemic. We sought to understand how rumors of commodity shortages cause panic buying even when most consumers are aware that there is no real shortage. We examined the role of prices in alleviating, or even preventing, panic buying caused by such rumors. Under some circumstances, flexible prices fail to do so and panic buying is the unique equilibrium outcome. In these circumstances, price floors prevent panic buying and lead to higher consumer surplus despite the possibility of rationing. Producer surplus may be higher as well.

Common Learning. In "Commonality of Information and Commonality of Beliefs," (Theoretical Economics, forthcoming), we studied how greater correlation in information available to the public---say, derived from more similar sources---can often lead to a divergence of beliefs about economically relevant events. Of course, greater commonality of information means that those who are optimistic also think that others are also optimistic. But it also means that those who are pessimistic think that others are also pessimistic. This pessimism the permeates the economy leading to overly cautious behavior, even stasis.

Disseminating Information. In our paper, "Spreading Information via Social Networks: an Irrelevance Result," we examine how a policymaker should spread information about a to the general public in order to induce efficient coordination---say the adoption of a new technology with positive externalities. The agents are connected via a social network. The planner informs a seed and then the information spreads via the network. While the structure of the network affects the rate of diffusion, we show that the rate of adoption is the same for all acyclic networks.

abstractText:
Space weather is the result of the coupling of energy from the solar wind into geospace and the myriad interactions between electric fields and charged particles with the geomagnetic field and neutral atmosphere. The resulting variability and disturbed conditions leads to harmful impacts on technological systems and even to risk to humans. Scientific imperatives and practical concerns converge in making space weather a rising priority for society and national planners. This collaborative project provides support for a consortium of four U.S. universities to continue the operations of a suite of High Frequency coherent-backscatter radars within the NSF Division of Atmospheric and Geospace Sciences (AGS). This extension will enable a broad range of research across the space science community. The U.S. consortium functions as part of the international Super Dual Auroral Radar Network (SuperDARN) which encompasses more than 35 radars distributed from mid through high to polar latitudes in both the northern and southern hemispheres. The leveraged benefits of the activities include student participation in the engineering and scientific tasks required to operate the network and to achieve the desired data products.

SuperDARN is well known for producing maps of the large-scale circulation of ionospheric plasma that can be compared in terms of scientific significance and practical utility to maps of winds and pressure systems in tropospheric weather. The radars observe a wide range of effects in the coupled magnetosphere-ionosphere thermosphere system that bear directly on understanding and modeling space weather events. The award will continue a program of continued observations while also achieving significant refurbishment of eleven U.S. radars located in North America and add the operations of two new radars in Iceland that are being built on separate support. It will also enable, with partial funding and by virtue of the availability of data, a broad range of research by the U.S. SuperDARN scientists on such new themes as convection in the inner magnetosphere, subauroral ionospheric convection, and solar flare impacts on the ionosphere. As a consequence of this award, the U.S. research community will be supplied with data from the entire set of SuperDARN radars and assisted in the application of SuperDARN data and data products. The award will provide new data products to the community include mapping of ionospheric plasma convection at much improved spatial resolution and techniques for applying machine learning to geospace datasets. In coordination with international collaborators simplified methods for data access will be developed that meet the emerging requirements by agencies and journals to make data discoverable and interoperable.

abstractText:
The layer of the atmosphere closest to the surface is known as the planetary boundary layer.  During the daytime, when the sun warms the surface and air rises and becomes turbulent, meteorologists refer to this layer as the convective boundary layer (CBL).  The height above the ground of the top of the CBL is variable and has relevance to thunderstorm initiation, precipitation, and pollutant concentration.  However, there is no simple way to provide continuous measurements of the height of the CBL over large areas.  This project will further investigate a method to retrieve the CBL top height by using the operational National Weather Service radar network.  These weather radars are sensitive enough to detect gradients in different airmasses, such as the more humid convective boundary layer and the drier air above that.  The significance of the work is through the development of a dataset that can be used to assess the ability of numerical models to simulate the convective boundary layer, and therefore practical weather phenomena.  The project also has a significant education and outreach component, with training for multiple graduate students, creation of features for a public television program, and implementation of a Research Experience for Teachers program.

The overarching goal of this project is to improve understanding of the evolution of the convective boundary layer top height (CBLH) using the clear-air remote sensing capabilities of the operational WSR-88D radar network.  S-band weather radar, in non-precipitating situations, can differentiate between biological returns (e.g. insects) and Bragg scatter (refractive index gradients) by using differential reflectivity to define the CBLH.  This technique would provide a significant increase in observations of CBLH due to the rapid updates and nationwide footprint of the WSR-88D network.  Five main activities are:  1) Develop monthly mean values of observed hourly daytime CBLH from at least 50 radars across the US over two distinct years (2014 and 2022) to explore similarities and differences in CBLH evolution, 2) Develop monthly mean values of predicted hourly daytime CBLH from the operational Rapid Refresh (RAP) model, 3) Calculate the difference between the radar observed CBLH and the RAP predicted CBLH, and explore reasons for the differences using all available observations, 4) Explore the ability of the differential reflectivity observations to estimate entrainment zone depth by comparing them to new rawinsonde observations, and 5) Study the late afternoon inversion layer separation and CBL descent using the observations and modeling derived above.

projectOutComesReport:
We spend our lives in the boundary layer, the atmospheric layer that is in direct contact with the Earth surface. The depth of the daytime portion of the boundary layer over land typically varies from a few tens of meters at sunrise to over 1000 m by late afternoon before falling back to a shallow depth around sunset. The boundary layer is arguably the most important layer for predicting whether thunderstorms will develop and for predicting air pollution concentration. Two fundamental parameters that characterize the boundary layer are its depth and the depth of the mixing zone at boundary layer top, called the entrainment zone.  

Our ability to observe the depth of the boundary layer historically has been limited to a few times a day from weather balloons. Dual-polarization upgrades to the U.S. national Doppler radar network in 2013 open the door to observing the daytime boundary layer every 10 minutes on most days at each of the 159 Doppler radars spread across the nation. 

We launched weather balloons every few hours throughout the daytime on numerous days to compare boundary layer depths indicated by the balloon observations with those estimated from dual-polarization Doppler radar.  Results show very good agreement, indicating that the radar can observe boundary layer depth throughout the daytime (Figure 1).  An algorithm to estimate boundary layer depth automatically from the radar observations was developed and applied to 2 years (2014 and 2022) of radar observations from 50 radar sites across the United States.  Results indicate that boundary layer depth is observed by the radars on roughly 2/3 of the days. Dual-polarization radars fail to observe boundary layer depth during rainfall and when vertical gradients in atmospheric moisture are small.  

We used the two years of radar-estimated boundary layer depth to calculate monthly mean maximum boundary layer depths and found that depths are a minimum in coastal regions and are a maximum in central states in summer (Figure 2).  Boundary layer depth also is influenced by large-scale weather systems and is increased by several hundred meters to the south of surface low pressure centers (Figure 3). Radar-derived boundary layer depth observations allow us to explore simultaneous boundary layer observations from across the United States and thereby expand our understanding of the mechanisms that drive boundary layer evolution.

We compared radar-derived boundary layer depth observations with those from a weather prediction model from 2022 to develop a very large data set and assess the model predictions of boundary layer structure.  Results show a consistent overprediction of boundary layer depth by the model (Figure 4), with errors in soil moisture explaining nearly half of the error.  This result highlights the importance of soil moisture observations for accurate boundary layer predictions, as well as the value of boundary layer observations in model verification and assessment. 

Strong mixing often occurs at boundary layer top where rising, warm air parcels interact with air from above the boundary layer.  This strong mixing layer is the entrainment zone, which has an outsized impact on boundary layer growth.  Results from comparisons with weather balloon observations show that dual-polarization Doppler radar observations can be used to estimate entrainment zone depth (Figure 5).  We determined entrainment zone depth for each day of 2022 from 50 radars across the United States.  The median entrainment zone depth is near 200 m in January and increases to near 600 m in July, with the largest depths present across the southeastern and southwestern United States (Figure 6).  This data set is the most spatiotemporally comprehensive data set of entrainment zone depth to date.  

When the observations of entrainment zone depth are combined with observations of boundary layer depth, our research shows that we routinely can observe two fundamental variables that describe boundary layer evolution from operational dual polarization Doppler radar.  We calculated radar-derived boundary layer depth observations for a case of torrential rainfall in Kentucky and the depth observations were used to help initialize a weather model.  The resulting simulations of heavy rainfall improved significantly in both location and amount when the boundary layer depth observations are included.  This work shows that radar-derived boundary layer observations can be used to improve forecasts of hazardous, high-impact weather.  

This research project trained two graduate students in boundary layer meteorology, weather radar, and data analysis methods, helping to develop the next generation of atmospheric scientists. Research results are being used in undergraduate and graduate education. Two high school science teachers were involved in the research and provided training to enhance their understanding of inquiry-based teaching methods, which has influenced their classroom practices.  

Results from this project show that we can observe key boundary layer characteristics routinely from dual-polarization radars.  This capability opens new avenues for boundary layer research.  The radar-derived boundary layer observations can be used to improve weather models and weather predictions.
